BRACE · Self-assessment

BRACE self-assessment and vendor evaluation

Use this worksheet to score the same 53 items as the BRACE sign-off checklist, across Build-time, Run-time, Agent, Configuration, and Ecosystem. The checklist holds the full requirements, the hard parts, fallbacks, and tradeoffs you can accept. The verification guide gives each item a test, the result to expect, and the evidence to keep.

How to use this

Assess a named release and environment. Or ask a vendor to show each requirement working in the setup you would actually use. Read the full checklist item before you score its short label below. Record what the agent team owns and what the platform or vendor owns, separately. Then score the combined evidence for the deployment.

Scoring and checklist outcomes

ScoreMeaningChecklist outcome
2 — YesThe full requirement is in place and shown with evidence.Pass
1 — PartialEvidence shows only part of the requirement, or only part of the deployment.Gap
0 — NoThe requirement is missing or can't be shown. A claim alone earns no credit.Gap
N/AThe feature or exposure doesn't exist, with evidence and an approved reason.N/A; leave out of the score denominator

A fallback earns 2 only when you can show it meets the requirement for the setup you assessed. Accepted risk does not turn a Partial or No into a Yes. Label details a provider doesn't share as hidden. Apply the model record and pinning rules in Configuration rule 1 and Configuration rule 5. Score the evidence you have, and never make up missing version details.

Priority gates

The Blocker/Required/Detection labels match the checklist's evidence requirements and lower-risk record gates. They do not authorize high-risk releases. Obs-T1/Obs-T2/Obs-T3 name observability requirements, not gates.

  • Blocker: Every applicable item must score 2 to meet this evidence requirement; retain each Partial or No as an open finding.
  • Required: Every applicable item must score 2, or have a written, approved risk acceptance.
  • Detection: For high-stakes or high-autonomy deployments, report every applicable score and retain Partial or No as an open finding. For lower-stakes deployments, a Partial or No needs a written, approved risk acceptance.

Rate the deployment's stakes and autonomy before you judge any gaps. Record owners, evidence, N/A approvals, and exceptions in the checklist records. Using a vendor's service doesn't make its part of a control N/A.

Reading your score

With all 53 items applicable, the maximum is 106 points. If some items have approved N/A results, use:

Coverage score = points earned / (2 × number of applicable items).

Report the number of applicable items, the N/A count, the points earned, and the denominator together. If no items apply, there is no score. Recheck the assessment scope instead of reporting readiness. Compare scores only when the scope and N/A decisions match.

The score tracks what you have shown is in place. It is not a security rating, and it does not approve a release. Report the number of open Blocker gaps and the status of Required and Detection exceptions separately. A high score can't make up for one blocker. A risk acceptance doesn't remove the gap from the score.

Finish with the checklist's final sign-off, including the next review date and what triggers a new review. Recheck the agent's powers on that schedule and remove access it no longer needs. Re-test after changes that matter.

Using this to evaluate a vendor

  • Ask for concrete artifacts: scoped access-token and delegation metadata, front/back audience checks, owner-approved tool versions, cross-tenant cache/task denials, alternative-path and outage tests, release/model manifests, drill results, and traces that show who did what.
  • Ask which controls the platform supplies and which your team must set up or build. A platform feature that is turned off in your deployment does not pass.
  • For hosted models, ask for the version details the provider shares. Keep them apart from pretraining history it doesn't share. For fine-tuning you run yourself, keep your job and dataset records, even if the base-model provider keeps theirs private.
  • Discuss the notes under the harder checklist items. Name the limits and the costs you accept. Then record any allowed risk acceptance, with an owner and approver.
  • Treat missing required evidence as a gap. If it blocks sign-off, cut the deployment's actual powers or choose an integration that can meet the requirement. Then re-test.

Assessing a vendor

Vendor worksheet reviewed: 2026-09-16; sources rechecked 2026-09-30. See the source review.

Use this worksheet to ask for, and record, evidence for each BRACE control. A product having a feature does not prove the control is turned on, set up correctly, or complete in your deployment. This worksheet does not rank vendors or give them checkmarks. Those claims would need a current comparison that others can repeat.

Use the 53-item checklist, its verification recipes, and the scoring worksheet above. Test the exact product version, plan, region, and configuration you will use. For each deployment, record demonstrated, partial, not demonstrated, or not applicable, with a reason. These are evidence results, not vendor rankings.

Per-control evidence matrix

BRACE controlChecklist itemsEvidence required from vendor and deployment owner
C1 — ArchitectureBuild-time rule 8–Build-time rule 9; Ecosystem rule 6Actual network routes, tenant isolation, egress and SSRF controls, and bypass test results. Calling a service "managed" does not prove where its boundary is.
C2 — Capability-scoped accessBuild-time rule 2–Build-time rule 4; Agent rule 1; Ecosystem rule 5–Ecosystem rule 8Separate acting-agent and delegated-subject identities, actual grants, front/back token audiences, supported exchanges, static-key exceptions, and measured revocation time, including caches and open work.
C3 — ContainerBuild-time rule 10–Build-time rule 11; Ecosystem rule 2Build provenance, checks against an approved signer, runtime isolation design, and the split of duties between customer and provider. Managed infrastructure may limit what you can inspect directly.
C4 — HarnessBuild-time rule 1; Build-time rule 5–Build-time rule 7; Build-time rule 12; Ecosystem rule 6; Ecosystem rule 8Versioned policies, enforcement on operation and arguments, approval replay tests, hard limits, and every other path that can run the same action.
C5 — DataRun-time rule 1–Run-time rule 4; Ecosystem rule 2–Ecosystem rule 7Input checks at each boundary, retrieval permissions, reviewed tool publication and rollback, scanner false positives/misses, and containment when injection detection misses.
C6 — MemoryRun-time rule 4–Run-time rule 6Scope enforcement, records of each entry's source and writer, revocation, cleanup, and how summaries and caches are handled.
C7 — BehavioralRun-time rule 8–Run-time rule 10; Agent rule 7; Ecosystem rule 12Written detection claims, measured misses and false alarms, identities of checker models, and responder drills.
C8 — Kill switchRun-time rule 11–Run-time rule 12; Agent rule 5; Ecosystem rule 9; Ecosystem rule 12Measured stop time across sub-agents, streams, queues, and disconnected workers. Reconciliation for effects that already happened.
C9 — Audit trailRun-time rule 3; Run-time rule 13–Run-time rule 14; Agent rule 4–Agent rule 5; Ecosystem rule 6; Ecosystem rule 10–Ecosystem rule 11Linked records of actions and results, protected retention, integrity checks against a separate trust anchor, and handling of unclear results and replays.
Obs-T1 — Six identity fieldsAgent rule 1–Agent rule 5; Agent rule 7; Configuration rule 1; Configuration rule 3–Configuration rule 4; Configuration rule 8; Ecosystem rule 10Accountable party, operational owner, tenant, type hash, instance ID, and trace context. Fields that only link records do not prove who an agent is.
Obs-T2 — Context sizeRun-time rule 7; Run-time rule 9; Configuration rule 8How full the context was, in tokens, at each decision. Include the counting method, limits of any estimate, and values marked unknown. Billing totals alone may not be enough.
Obs-T3 — Parent/prompt provenanceAgent rule 6; Configuration rule 8Parent-child trace links, and the prompt the parent passed (or a protected reference to it). Show that links survive handoffs and that access is controlled.

Ecosystem rule 1 and the Configuration items (Configuration rule 1–Configuration rule 8) apply across the whole matrix, including model records and the history of training you run yourself. A vendor may cover only part of an item. Name who builds and checks the rest. No product listing changes the checklist's Blocker/Required/Detection rules.

MCP gateway deployment evidence

Record the deployment pattern: internal HTTP, public third-party service, or local stdio. Request the protocol/extension versions, owner-approved tool inventory, publication/config propagation and rollback evidence, and policy tests for direct, dynamic, CLI/code-mode, and wrapper calls. Verify gateway and backend credentials separately. Test private cache/task/state isolation across tenants and after revocation; test Apps sandbox/CSP/bridge and task cancellation where enabled. An internal mTLS design is one option. A public service may require controls on agent egress and credential access instead; a local server needs host/sandbox enforcement. A clean metadata scan or a project-specific gateway conformance claim is not a BRACE pass.

Reference designs and standards

OWASP Agent Control Standard (ACS) defines portable runtime control hooks. It works alongside BRACE's deployment review. Check framework support and maturity before you rely on a given integration.

The Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit's MCP Security Gateway 1.0 specification (pinned revision 580344a, 2026-09-25) labels itself Draft. It describes interception, scanning, authentication, fingerprinting, audit, and conformance requirements. Written requirements do not show that any implementation has been independently tested against them. Run the relevant tests on the actual implementation.

A gateway circuit breaker does not, by itself, stop remote child agents. A fingerprint of a tool's description and schema does not catch hidden changes to remote code. HMAC authentication does not supply all six BRACE identity fields. Check each of these limits on its own. Don't map one feature to a whole control.
